### The Veyr

On the planet Nhal, where ammonia seas lie beneath a crushing hydrogen sky, the Veyr drifts through the dark like a piece of night that has learned to change its shape.

It has no head, limbs, eyes, or skin. Its body is a loose, three-dimensional net of dark mineral struts, some as fine as hair and others broad as blades. The net may stretch for hundreds of meters, with great empty spaces between its strands. Tiny pale knots glimmer at the crossings—not organs, exactly, but places where the lattice’s chemistry is most active. The whole creature is buoyant in the dense atmosphere, turning so slowly that a change in its posture can take hours.

The Veyr is not made of cells. Its living pattern is built into the way its mineral framework holds and moves charged particles. Where one part of the lattice meets a different chemical current, reactions release energy. The Veyr uses that energy to repair its struts, alter its buoyancy, and slowly reshape itself. It does not swim by beating anything. Instead, it grows one side denser while loosening the other, and the planet’s winds carry it in the direction it has chosen.

It has no eyes, but it can detect disturbances across its entire body. A change in the pressure of the air, a distant electrical storm, or a faint chemical plume from a volcanic vent alters the lattice’s electrical behavior. The Veyr “senses” these changes as patterns of tension and charge. A nearby creature might be, to it, not a visible shape but a sudden, complicated disturbance moving through the surrounding world.

Its thoughts are slow and spread out. There is no central brain: signals travel through the net as waves of altered conductivity. Memories persist as lasting changes in the struts’ arrangement, like old paths worn into a landscape. What it experiences as a single thought might take several minutes to cross its body. It may remember a storm not as an image, but as a particular sequence of pressures and charges that once bent it nearly to breaking.

When two Veyr meet, they do not touch in any familiar sense. Their lattices drift close, and each senses the other’s changing electrical field. They may exchange patterns—a warning, perhaps, or a trace of where the chemical currents are richest. To an observer, this looks like two drifting tangles briefly twisting around one another before separating.

A Veyr reproduces when a violent storm tears off a portion of its lattice. Most fragments decay. But if one lands in a suitable current, it can slowly build itself outward, drawing minerals from the air and sea. Whether the new Veyr is a child, a severed part, or simply the old creature continuing somewhere else is not a question the species could answer in any human way. To the Veyr, a self may be less like a body than a pattern that has not yet finished changing.

There is no head, front, or back. The oruun does not face the world; it is immersed in it. It detects its surroundings through tiny shifts in pressure, temperature, and chemical composition, and through the planet’s magnetic field. A warm updraft on one side, or a trace of a useful gas far below, changes the arrangement of its filaments. The creature turns by reorganizing itself, gradually drawing more of its body toward the new condition. What looks like drifting cloud is, to the oruun, movement with purpose.

On the moonless planet **Vey**, beneath a ceiling of ice, floats the **unmoored choir**.

It has no front or back, no head, no limbs, and no enclosing skin. Its shape is full of holes. Water, dissolved gases, and tiny mineral grains pass through it freely.

Vey’s ocean is a cold, dense mixture of ammonia and water. The choir’s strands are mineral-reinforced polymers, threaded with thousands of sealed reaction pockets. Each pocket can exchange chemicals with its neighbours, but none commands the rest. There is no brain. Instead, a chemical change in one region can travel through the lattice as a slow wave, altering the behaviour of distant pockets. To an observer, the whole creature seems to think by changing its shape.

It feeds on contrasts. Near the ocean floor, warm vents release hydrogen and other reduced compounds; closer to the underside of the ice, photochemistry supplies oxidizing molecules. The choir drifts between these chemical layers, absorbing substances across almost its entire surface. When one region encounters a richer supply, the lattice stiffens there. Elsewhere, it loosens and lets the current carry it around. Its movement is not a stroke or a crawl, but a gradual rearrangement—more like a shape changing its mind.

The creature has no eyes. It detects the world as differences in acidity, dissolved gases, pressure, and the faint electrical effects of moving ions. A sudden change travels through it in a ripple. If the ripple reaches enough of its active pockets, the choir folds inward, or turns a broad surface toward a chemical plume. When startled, it releases a cloud of fine mineral flakes that confuse chemical traces and drift away like pale snow.

Its life unfolds slowly. A single migration between the vents and the ice may take months. During lean seasons, the choir contracts into a dense knot and reduces its activity almost to a standstill. In better conditions, it unfurls again, extending new lattice into the current.

It reproduces by coming apart. In a safe place, its strands weaken along several lines, and the lattice separates into drifting fragments. Most fragments die. A successful one must land where the chemistry supports it, then grow until its pockets begin to pulse in coordination. Only then does it become a new choir—though there is no exact moment when a fragment stops being part of its parent and starts being itself.

When several choirs drift near one another, their chemical waves sometimes fall into step. For hours, their lattices flex together across the dark ocean, exchanging no words and perhaps no information at all. From a distance, it looks like a single enormous creature slowly changing its mind.
